item.title: Escaping a downward spiral for science and public accountability | Science
item.description: In late July, Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), released Science—A Golden Age, setting forth a strategy to revitalize US research and innovation for the 21st century. The report is a response to what it calls “a systematic breakdown in the lines of accountability that align the scientific enterprise with the public interest.” The pace of innovation in the United States is too slow, it argues, harming the country’s economic growth and competitiveness. In what it characterizes as the artificial intelligence (AI) “race,” in particular, the report observes that China is uncomfortably close. It asserts that the federal funding infrastructure is beset with administrative burdens like commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion, which constrain investigators and prioritize the wrong values. Meanwhile, universities, which the report deems “legacy institutions,” are too ossified to meet the nation’s innovation demands. Rather, they are “entrenched interests” that are no longer sufficiently accountable to the public interest.

item.title: Prevent a drone e-waste crisis | Science
item.description: Drones are rapidly becoming routine tools in surveillance, inspection, agriculture, logistics, emergency response, reconnaissance, and warfare (1). The global commercial and military drone markets are projected to reach US$54.6 billion and US$22.8 billion, respectively, by 2030 (2, 3). However, end-of-life governance has not kept pace. In 2022, the world generated 62 million tonnes of e-waste, only 22.3% of which was formally collected and recycled (4). Planning for retired drone management must account for fire, materials recovery, and information-security risks.

item.title: Free inquiry depends on freedom of movement | Science
item.description: Starting in May 2025, the US government implemented an immigration policy that targeted noncitizen researchers for visa denials, visa revocations, detention, and deportation on the basis of the topics and findings of their work (1). In response, scholars and civil society groups at the Coalition for Independent Technology Research (CITR) documented the policy’s effects on their research and sued the State Department, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Justice Department to stay the policy (2). Scholarly societies, including the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) (3) and the Association of Internet Researchers (AOIR) (4) issued public statements in support of academics’ freedom of movement. In July 2026, a federal court suspended the policy (5), marking a victory for scientific progress (6). However, threats to freedom of movement remain a powerful tool for repressive governments to force and entice scholars into submission. Scholars and administrators should continue to defend the integrity of science by defending the right to freedom of movement.
